reports.title: Max Stack, Job Scheduler, and API Blocking Problems

rounds.name: Round 2: System design, job scheduler (one-time and recurring jobs)

items.title: Max Stack
items.question: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, peekMax and popMax (remove the largest element; if there are several, the one closest to the top).
items.short: Keep the stack as a doubly linked list so any node can be removed in O(1), plus a TreeMap from value to the nodes holding that value (newest last). push/pop/top are O(1) on the list plus O(log n) on the TreeMap. peekMax is lastKey(). popMax takes the newest node of the largest key, unlinks it from the list, and cleans up the map. Everything is O(log n).
followups: Make every op O(1) amortized except popMax? (Two-stack variants; prove it's impossible to get all O(1): you'd sort in O(n).)
Thread-safe version? (One lock around both structures; operations are short.)
MinMaxStack, or popMax on a queue instead of a stack?

items.title: API request blocker (rate limit + block)
items.source: Sep 9 report ("API Blocking"). Exact wording wasn't reported; this is the common form of the question.
items.question: Allow each client at most `limit` requests per `window` seconds. A client that goes over is blocked for `blockFor` seconds. Implement `allow(clientId, timestamp)`.
items.short: Per client, keep a queue of accepted timestamps and a blockedUntil time. On a request: if blocked, reject. Otherwise drop timestamps older than the window from the front; if the queue still has `limit` entries, block the client (blockedUntil = now + blockFor), clear its history and reject; else record the timestamp and accept. Amortized O(1) per call, O(clients × limit) memory.
followups: Switch to a token bucket: what changes? (Refill tokens lazily from elapsed time; no queue.)
Different limits per API key tier? (A config lookup; key = (client, endpoint).)
Out-of-order timestamps? (Insert into the right place, or accept small skew.)

items.title: Job scheduler (one-time and recurring), in-memory
items.source: Sep 9 report ("Job Scheduler"). The same idea underlies the system design round.
items.question: Support schedule(job, time), scheduleRecurring(job, first, interval), cancel(job) and runUntil(now), returning the runs that are due, in order.
items.short: A min-heap of upcoming runs ordered by (time, jobId). runUntil pops everything due; a recurring run pushes its next occurrence back in. One map from each job to its live upcoming run handles cancel and replace: cancel removes the job from the map, rescheduling points it at the new run, and a popped run that isn't the job's current entry is skipped (lazy deletion). schedule is O(log n), cancel O(1).
followups: Implement it with real threads. (DelayQueue / Condition.awaitNanos; handle spurious wakeups.)
Cron expressions instead of intervals? (A function nextRun(after) replaces time + interval.)
Priorities among jobs due at the same time? (Add priority to the comparator.)

items.title: LRU Cache → Progressive LRU (AI coding round)
items.source: Sep 7 report, Round 3 (AI coding: progressive LRU). AI is meant as an assistant, not a replacement.
items.question: Implement an LRU cache, then extend it step by step (typical steps: expiry/TTL, thread safety, size-based capacity, metrics/eviction callbacks).
items.short: Step 1: HashMap<key, Node> + doubly linked list, with the most recently used at the head; get and put are O(1). Step 2 (TTL): store expireAt in each node; get checks it lazily; put on a full cache drops expired entries before evicting the LRU. A min-heap by expireAt avoids the O(n) sweep. Step 3 (threads): one lock (simple, correct), then striped or segmented locks, or ConcurrentHashMap plus approximate LRU for scale. Step 4: weight-based capacity, eviction listener, hit/miss stats. Keep each step's tests green before moving on.
followups: Why not a read-write lock? (get changes recency, so it's a write.)
LRU vs LFU vs W-TinyLFU: when does LRU do badly? (A scan pollutes the cache; frequency-aware policies resist it.)
Distributed cache: consistent hashing, replication, hot keys.

items.title: Find Leaves of Binary Tree (LC 366) → general graph
items.question: Repeatedly remove all leaves of a binary tree and return the values removed in each round. Follow-up: the structure is a general graph. How does the approach change?
items.short: Tree: a node is removed in round = its height (leaf = 0). One post-order DFS computes the height and appends the node to out[height]: O(n). Graph: there's no root, nodes can have several parents, and there may be cycles. Height-by-DFS double-counts shared children (memoize) and loops forever on cycles. Use Kahn's algorithm on reversed edges: start from nodes with no children, remove them, and decrement their parents' child counts level by level. Nodes on (or above) a cycle never become leaves; report them.
followups: Return the remaining cycle nodes too. (Everything with remaining children > 0.)
Edges arrive as a stream (dependency updates)? (Incremental counts; recompute affected layers.)
Where does this show up for real? (Build systems and package managers: which modules can be built or deleted first.)

items.title: Robot in an unexplored grid
items.source: Aug 11 report, Round 4: rotate, move forward, detect walls, reposition to explored cells; find a path to the target.
items.question: The grid isn't given. A robot API lets you rotate, move forward (reporting walls), check for the target, and jump back to explored cells. Find the shortest path from the start to the target.
items.short: Build your own map in coordinates relative to the start (the start is (0,0)). Because reposition lets you jump to any explored cell, you can run BFS directly: pop a cell, reposition there, and for each direction not yet known, turn to face it and try moveForward. If it moves, record the neighbour at distance + 1 and reposition back. The first time isTarget() is true, the BFS depth is the shortest path. Without reposition: DFS with backtracking to map the reachable area, then BFS on the map.
followups: What if turning costs time? (State = (cell, facing); Dijkstra or 0-1 BFS.)
What if the grid is huge and the target is close? (BFS stops early; A* once the target is known.)
Make the exploration resumable after a crash? (Persist the map.)

items.title: Supply drop: nearest supply, then a constrained route (AI-assisted graph round)
items.source: Aug 11 report, Round 2. Part 1 was reported; part 2 "reasoned about a transformed version of the graph with additional structural constraints" and wasn't remembered exactly. Part II here is the most likely shape; the other likely twists are covered below.
items.question: Locations connected by routes; some have supplies. Part 1: distance from the landing location to the nearest suitable supply location. Part 2: a harder version on a transformed graph with extra constraints.
items.short: Part 1 is single-source shortest path: Dijkstra from the landing site (BFS if routes are unweighted), stopping at the first supply location popped. Part 2's 'transformed graph' is almost certainly a **state graph**: each node becomes (location, extra state). Examples: (location, hasSupplies) for 'must visit a supply first', (location, fuelLeft) for limited fuel, (location, stopsUsed) for a hop limit, or reversed edges for 'distance from every location to the nearest supply'. Run the same Dijkstra or BFS over the states.
followups: Return the actual route. (Keep a parent pointer per state; walk back from the goal state.)
Supplies get used up (each depot serves one team)? (Assignment / min-cost matching, not shortest path.)
Distances change while the team is moving? (Re-run from the current location; incremental algorithms like D* Lite.)

items.title: CI build pipeline: minimum total time (topological sort)
items.source: Aug 11 report ("CI/CD, Job Scheduling"). A natural coding question for a CI/CD team; also the core of the CI scheduler design.
items.question: Jobs with durations and dependencies run in parallel. When does the pipeline finish? Detect cycles.
items.short: Kahn's topological sort. A job's earliest start = max finish time of its dependencies; the answer is the max finish time (the critical path). If fewer than n jobs get processed, there's a cycle → -1. O(V + E).
followups: Detect *which* jobs form the cycle. (DFS with colours; report the back edge.)
Minimum time with k workers. (Heuristic; explain NP-hardness.)
Jobs can be cached; how do you decide a job can be skipped? (Hash of inputs + toolchain.)

items.title: CI/CD and developer experience: domain questions
items.source: Aug 11 report, Round 1: questions on continuous integration, continuous delivery, package management and developer-infrastructure concepts. Senior Staff needed stronger domain depth here.
items.question: Be ready for rapid-fire domain questions on CI, CD, package management and developer infrastructure.
items.short: Know the vocabulary and the trade-offs, and anchor answers in your own systems. CI: trunk-based development, fast feedback, merge queues, hermetic and cached builds, flaky-test management. CD: artifact promotion, progressive delivery (canary, blue/green, feature flags), automated rollback, DORA metrics. Packages: semantic versioning, lockfiles, dependency resolution (diamond conflicts), private registries, monorepo vs polyrepo. Supply-chain security: SBOM, signing, provenance (SLSA). DevEx: build/test latency and queue time as the north-star metrics.
items.answer:
### Continuous integration
- **CI** = every change is merged to the main line frequently and verified automatically (build + tests). Goal: catch integration problems in minutes, not at release time.
- **Trunk-based development** vs long-lived branches: short-lived branches + feature flags keep merges small.
- **Merge queue:** PRs are tested on top of the latest main (and of each other) before merging, so main stays green with many concurrent merges. Batch and bisect on failure.
- **Fast feedback:** test sharding, running only **affected targets** (build-graph analysis), **remote build caching** (Bazel/Gradle: cache key = hash of inputs + toolchain), **hermetic builds** (no network, pinned toolchains → reproducible and cacheable).
- **Flaky tests:** detect with re-runs, track a flake rate per test, quarantine with an owner and an SLA; never let flakiness train people to ignore red builds.
- **Test pyramid:** many unit tests, fewer integration tests, few end-to-end tests.

### Continuous delivery / deployment
- **Delivery** = every green build is *releasable* (deploy is one click). **Deployment** = every green build is deployed automatically.
- **Build once, promote the same artifact** through dev → staging → prod (immutable, versioned, signed). Never rebuild per environment; configuration is separate.
- **Strategies:** rolling, **blue/green** (switch traffic between two environments; instant rollback), **canary** (1% → 10% → 100% with automated analysis of error rate and latency), **feature flags** (decouple deploy from release; kill switch), shadow traffic.
- **Rollback vs roll forward;** database migrations with expand/contract (backward-compatible schema changes first).
- **GitOps:** the desired state lives in Git (e.g. Argo CD reconciles the cluster to it); every change is auditable.
- **DORA metrics:** deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, time to restore.

### Package management
- **Semantic versioning** MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH; ranges (`^1.2.0`, `~1.2.0`); pre-releases.
- **Lockfiles** pin the exact resolved tree for reproducible installs (package-lock, poetry.lock, Gradle lockfiles); update them deliberately with bots (Dependabot/Renovate).
- **Dependency resolution:** the **diamond dependency** problem (A needs C 1.x, B needs C 2.x). Maven picks the "nearest wins", npm nests copies, pip/Poetry use backtracking SAT-like solvers, Go uses minimal version selection.
- **Private registries / proxies** (Artifactory, Nexus, CodeArtifact): caching, availability, internal packages, license and vulnerability scanning; protection against **dependency confusion** (pin scopes and namespaces).
- **Monorepo vs polyrepo:** atomic cross-project changes and a single version policy vs independent release cycles; monorepos need build-graph tooling (Bazel, Pants, Nx) and code ownership.

### Supply-chain security
SBOM (what's inside each artifact), artifact **signing** (Sigstore/cosign), **provenance** attestations (SLSA levels), pinned base images, secret scanning, least-privilege CI tokens (OIDC instead of long-lived keys), isolating untrusted PR builds.

### Developer experience as a platform
North-star metrics: **CI wait + run time** for the PR loop, local build time, deploy lead time, flake rate. Paved roads: golden templates, self-service pipelines, good error messages. Internal developer portals (service catalog, ownership).

### Linking to your background (useful for the leveling conversation)
You've built platforms where correctness at scale, policy enforcement and multi-team adoption mattered (compliance, access management, workflow engines). Map those to CI/CD: policy-as-code for pipelines (who can deploy what), audit trails, workflow orchestration (pipelines are DAG workflows, like the BPMN engine work), and guardrails. Then be honest about where you'd ramp up, and show how fast you learn a domain.
followups: What's the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment?
How would you cut median PR CI time from 40 min to 10?
Explain how a remote build cache decides a cache hit.
How do you safely roll out a breaking database schema change?

items.title: AI-assisted coding rounds: how to run them
items.source: Aug 11 report, Round 2 (had to reason without AI in part 2) and Sep 7 report, Round 3 (AI is an assistant, not a replacement).
items.question: How should you use the AI assistant in LinkedIn's AI coding rounds?
items.short: You own the solution; the AI types faster. Restate the problem and design the algorithm yourself, out loud, before prompting. Use the AI for boilerplate, parsing long scenarios, test cases, and the API details you'd look up anyway. Review every line, run tests, and narrate what you're checking. Be ready at any moment to continue without it: the interviewer may switch it off to test your reasoning (it happened in the graph round).
items.answer:
### A loop that works
1. **Understand (no AI):** restate the problem, identify the core structure (graph? interval? cache?), list edge cases, agree on input/output.
2. **Design (no AI):** state the algorithm and complexity in 2–3 sentences. Get a nod from the interviewer.
3. **Generate (AI):** ask for a skeleton matching *your* design, plus tests (including edge cases you listed). Be specific: "Java, no lambdas, Dijkstra with a PriorityQueue of long[]".
4. **Verify (you):** read the code, run the tests, add a tricky case. Explain any fix you make. Never accept code you can't explain.
5. **Extend:** for each new requirement, say the design change first, then prompt.

### What interviewers score
- Problem decomposition and the algorithm choice: **yours**, not the AI's.
- Judgement: catching wrong or over-complicated AI output; knowing when to just write it yourself.
- Testing discipline and communication.

### Practice plan with this page
- Solve each focus problem once **without** AI to make sure the algorithms are yours (especially Dijkstra / state graphs and BFS).
- Then redo two of them with an AI assistant, timing yourself, practising specific prompts and reviewing the output.
- Rehearse the "explain without AI" moment: for Supply Drop II, explain the state graph on a whiteboard in under 2 minutes.
followups: What would you do if the AI's solution passes the tests but you don't understand one part? (Don't ship it: read it, simplify it, or rewrite that part.)

items.title: Staff behavioral + the leveling conversation
items.source: Aug 11 report, Round 1 (manager): scope stories led to a Staff vs Senior Staff leveling discussion; Senior Staff required deeper domain expertise in the team's area. Sep 7 report also had behavioral questions.
items.question: Behavioral questions with a manager, where your examples also decide the level (Staff vs Senior Staff).
items.short: Prepare 6–8 stories with clear scope (team → org → company), your specific role, the hard decision or conflict, and measurable impact. For leveling: show scope (multi-org influence, multi-year vision) **and** depth in the team's domain. Research the team's domain beforehand (CI/CD and developer infrastructure here) and connect your experience to it explicitly. If they raise level, ask what evidence would support the higher level and offer it.
items.answer:
### Story bank (STAR, ~2 minutes each; lead with the result)
| Theme | Prompt you'll get | Story to pick |
|---|---|---|
| Scope & vision | "Tell me about the largest-scope thing you led." | A cross-org architecture you defined and drove to adoption; numbers (scale, adoption, revenue). |
| Ambiguity | "A problem with no clear owner or solution." | How you framed it, the options, the decision record. |
| Influence without authority | "You had to convince other teams." | Getting product, engineering and go-to-market aligned on one architecture. |
| Technical depth | "The hardest technical problem you solved." | A scale or correctness problem with real trade-offs (e.g. billions of items under policy). |
| Conflict / disagreement | "You disagreed with a leader or peer." | The data you brought, how you disagreed and then committed. |
| Failure | "Something that went wrong." | Own it, the fix, what you changed in the process afterwards. |
| Mentoring / multiplying | "How do you grow other engineers?" | Architecture forums, reviews, people you levelled up. |
| Delivery under pressure | "A deadline or incident." | What you cut, how you managed risk. |

Use your strongest recent material: architecture you defined and drove across orgs (access management/ABAC building blocks, archive at billion-file scale, workflow automation with embedded AI agents, AI guardrails), with concrete numbers where you have them.

### The leveling conversation
- Staff vs Senior Staff usually differ in **breadth of influence** (a group of teams vs a whole org/company) **and** in being *the* recognized expert in an area.
- The feedback in the report was: scope was there, **domain depth** in CI/CD was the gap. Prepare for both:
  1. One story clearly at Senior Staff scope (multi-org, multi-year).
  2. A crisp explanation of how your experience maps onto *their* domain (pipelines = DAG workflow orchestration; policy and compliance = deployment guardrails and audit; platform adoption = developer experience).
  3. A short, honest ramp-up plan for the domain gaps (first 90 days).
- It's fine to ask: "What would you need to see to be confident at the Senior Staff level?"

### Questions to ask them
Biggest developer-experience pain point today? How do they measure CI/CD success (queue time, flake rate, DORA)? Build vs buy (GitHub Actions, Buildkite, internal)? What would a Staff engineer own in the first 6 months?
followups: Why this team / domain? (Have a real answer that connects to platform and developer leverage.)
What would you do in your first 90 days?
